title: Ray Model of Light: Reflection and Refraction
seo_title: Secondary 1 Science: Reflection and Refraction of Light Worksheets with Answers
standard_text: Describe the ray model of light; describe reflection by smooth and rough surfaces and the uses of plane and curved mirrors; investigate the image formed by a plane mirror and that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; explain refraction as caused by a change in the speed of light and describe the dispersion of white light by a prism; recognise effects of infrared and ultraviolet radiation and light pollution (summary of the MOE Lower Secondary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 1 science worksheets for Singapore students on the ray model of light: the law of reflection, plane mirror images, curved mirrors, refraction and dispersion. With answers.
key_big: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
key_sub: Measure both angles from the normal.
body_html:
How to think about it

Light travels in straight lines, shown as rays. It reflects off surfaces and refracts when its speed changes.

  • Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
  • Plane mirror image: upright, same size, laterally inverted, virtual, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
  • Light slows down entering glass or water and bends towards the normal; it speeds up and bends away when it leaves.
  • A prism splits white light into colours: dispersion. Infrared and ultraviolet are invisible radiation.
Example

A ray makes 30° with the mirror surface. Angle of reflection?

Angle of incidence = 90° − 30° = 60°

Answer: 60°

Example

You stand 2 m from a plane mirror. How far are you from your image?

The image is 2 m behind the mirror

Answer: 4 m

Common mistakes

  • Measuring angles from the mirror instead of the normal.
  • Saying light speeds up when it enters glass. It slows down.
  • Saying a plane mirror image is upside down. It is upright but laterally inverted.
  • Thinking rough surfaces do not reflect. They reflect diffusely.

faq.q: Why are angles measured from the normal?
faq.a: The normal is a line at 90° to the surface. Measuring from it makes the law of reflection the same for every surface.

faq.q: Why does a straw look bent in water?
faq.a: Light from the straw refracts as it leaves the water, so the part in the water appears higher than it is.
Left and right are swapped in a plane mirror image.

items.q: A ray of light hits a plane mirror. The angle between the ray and the mirror surface is 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
items.e: Angles are measured from the normal: 90° − 35° = 55°, and i = r.

items.e: The normal is at 90° to the mirror, so 90° − 55° = 35°.

items.q: Why do we see objects that do not give out their own light?

items.e: Most objects are seen by reflected light.

items.q: Which kind of reflecting surface is used in a make-up mirror that magnifies?

items.q: A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is. Which effect of light explains this?

items.q: What is the law of reflection?
c: Angles are measured from the mirror.
The angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.
items.e: The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal lie in the same plane.

items.q: What does a ray in a ray diagram represent?
c: the path along which light travels
items.e: Rays are straight lines with arrows.

items.q: A straw in a glass of water looks bent. Which effect of light explains this?

items.q: A prism splits white light into seven colours. Which effect of light explains this?

items.q: What is the difference between regular and diffuse reflection?
c: A smooth surface reflects parallel rays in one direction; a rough surface scatters them in many directions.

items.q: Which kind of reflecting surface is used in a dressing-table mirror?

items.q: Which kind of reflecting surface is used in the reflector behind a torch bulb?

items.e: New distance to the mirror = 0.5 m, so image distance = 2 × 0.5 = 1 m.

items.q: What is dispersion?
c: the bouncing of light off a mirror
the splitting of white light into its colours by a prism
the dimming of light at night
the bending of a ray along the normal
items.e: Different colours refract by different amounts.

items.q: In the spectrum made by a prism, which colour comes after red?
items.e: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

items.q: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block at an angle. What happens to the light?
c: It speeds up and bends towards the normal.
It slows down but does not bend.
It slows down and bends away from the normal.
It slows down and bends towards the normal.
items.e: Light changes speed when it enters a different medium, so it bends (refracts) unless it travels along the normal.

items.q: What is light pollution?

items.q: Why are emergency vehicles often yellow with reflective strips?

items.e: Reflection for safety.

items.q: A fisherman aims his spear below where a fish appears to be. Why?

items.q: Why does the bottom of a swimming pool look closer than it is?
c: Light from the bottom refracts as it leaves the water.

items.q: Why does a pinhole camera make an upside-down image?

items.e: Law of reflection.

items.q: A torch shines on a white wall and on a mirror. Why can a person standing to the side see the spot on the wall but not on the mirror?
